extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly — general public, gardeners/horticulturists, and lay readers interested in natural history and health
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and observations about determining the relative hardiness of plants (including sources of variation, pitfalls of casual observation, and recommendations for systematic reporting). Also includes a short medical explanation defining the common cold and its mucous-membrane basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of varieties (not just species)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The question may be easily asked, Wherein lies the difference between a variety and a species? but the answer evidently is not so easy, when we consider that every individual plant varies in a degree from all other plants; and, to render it still more difficult, we find botanists very properly ignoring the existence of varieties that may have individual characteristics invaluable to the planter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess hardiness at the level of varieties and individual plants, not only at the species or genus level. Many valuable and noteworthy traits affecting hardiness are variety-specific; ignoring varieties leads to misleading generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate (not latitude) as the governing factor
rubrics_metrics.description: “Latitude, moreover, we find, is only one factor, and a very vague one, in the problem of determining the relative hardiness of plants. Climate is the real governing element — climate, that varies with the special conditions of every valley and hill-top.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether a plant will be hardy in a location, use local climate and site-specific conditions (temperature ranges, moisture regimes, seasonality) rather than latitude alone as the principal metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microclimate and local environmental conditions matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations that ‘the varying and complex conditions of the environment of any given plant are difficult to understand’ and that plants a few feet from each other, or within a few miles, may behave very differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate micro-site details (shelter, exposure, proximity to water, shade, hilltop vs valley, soil drainage, local wind patterns). Even small differences in microclimate can change hardiness outcomes; therefore assessments must record precise location/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and regional origin affect hardiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples showing that Japanese plants can resemble American ones yet differ in hardiness; and that plants from specific regions (Pacific coast, mountains, Amoor River) show differing performance when moved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include provenance (native range, elevation, local climate of origin) when evaluating a plant's likely hardiness. Plants from similar latitude but different climatic regimes (oceanic vs continental, mountain vs lowland) may not be interchangeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation and management influence perceived hardiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted differences such as evergreens doing better, and being more hardy, in cultivated European settings versus deciduous trees in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between wild/native hardiness and performance under cultivation; husbandry, sheltering, and cultural practices can change observed hardiness and must be recorded when comparing regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual plant condition (e.g., ripening of wood) affects winter survival
rubrics_metrics.description: The author’s expert explanations that sometimes one plant of the same species survives while a neighboring one dies — ‘One did not ripen its wood as well as the other,’ though this does not always fully explain outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing hardiness, record plant health metrics (growth stage, wood maturity/seasonal ripening, prior stress). Individual physiological state can be decisive and may explain discrepancies among nearby specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macroclimatic modifiers must be considered (ocean currents, moisture, temperature equability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion that oceanic currents, the trend of mountain-ranges, moisture and a more equable temperature can make climates of the same latitude differ markedly and influence plant hardiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate large-scale climatic modifiers (e.g., Gulf Stream, maritime vs continental influence, elevation-related temperature regimes) into hardiness assessments rather than relying on simple latitudinal zones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralizing from limited or unsystematic experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The article warns that ‘experience is now being purchased too dearly, and it is, moreover, not of a sufficiently varied character. Hundreds and thousands of plants are killed every year under very similar circumstances, and it seems evident that human intelligence should be sufficient to compass some method of reducing this loss to a minimum.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat isolated anecdotes and small-sample observations with caution. Reliable hardiness conclusions require broad, systematic, and replicated observations across varied sites and years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic recording and centralized reporting of hardiness data
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation: ‘The proper sources of these reports would be botanic gardens... the superintendents and gardeners... might be directed to make careful investigations and fill up printed forms month by month on the behavior of plants in different localities. Above all, private individuals... should be encouraged to investigate in the same systematic way and report to the central repository.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt standardized, periodic reporting (e.g., monthly printed forms) collected in a central repository (botanic gardens/arboreta) to create compact published tables of actual hardiness. Encourage both institutional and lay contributors to ensure varied, reliable data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grafting compatibility and horticultural behavior as practical indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Example that Retinosporas graft well on American arbor-vitae stocks and behave similarly in hardiness despite botanical distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed horticultural compatibility and behavioral similarity (grafting success, cultivation response) as practical signals of functional similarity in hardiness, while still noting botanical differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about short-term acclimatization
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The so-called acclimatization of plants... Natural selection carried on for hundreds and thousands of years may accomplish a change of nature of this sort, but, under ordinary limitations of time, the attempt to acclimatize, in this sense, is practically futile.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that protecting and gradually exposing tender plants in the short term will reliably render them hardy. Distinguish between long-term evolutionary adaptation and short-term management; treat claims of rapid acclimatization skeptically and verify experimentally over many seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of common cold as a mild febrile mucous-membrane inflammation
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the first place, we must be paradoxical, and affirm that it is not a cold at all. It is rather a heat... it is a form of fever, but... of a very mild type... It is certainly in the majority of instances due to the effects of cold playing upon some portion of the body, and reacting upon the mucous membrane through the intervention of the nervous apparatus.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing a ‘cold,’ look for systemic febrile signs (rigor/shivering, raised body temperature) and inflammation of the mucous membrane (Schneiderian membrane). Understand that the term ‘cold’ refers to a mild inflammatory/fever process often precipitated indirectly by exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand mucous-membrane anatomy and function in pathogenesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation that the Schneiderian membrane’s functions are to equalize temperature, moisten, and filter inhaled air; it is richly vascular and thus easily congested leading to inflammation constituting a cold in the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any explanation, prevention, or treatment of common colds should account for mucous membrane physiology (large surface area, vascularity, mucus secretion, hairs for filtering). This helps explain susceptibility and symptom development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predisposition factors: chronic mucous-membrane congestion and digestive disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement that ‘people who have what is called an irritable mucous membrane are so susceptible of cold. They have, in fact, a chronically congested mucous membrane, which, however, is usually associated with and dependent upon a disordered digestion.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating risk or recurrent colds, consider underlying predispositions such as chronically congested/irritable mucous membranes and systemic conditions (e.g., digestive disorders) that may increase susceptibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation: nervous mediation rather than simple local cooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that ‘a cold is not produced by cold air acting upon the surface which suffers... it is... due to the effects of cold playing upon some portion of the body, and reacting upon the mucous membrane through the intervention of the nervous apparatus.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic causal models that attribute colds solely to local tissue chilling. Consider reflexive/nervous responses and systemic interactions when explaining onset; prevention strategies should address whole-body responses as well as local exposure.
